items.name: Vinča culture
items.description: A Late Neolithic / Early Copper Age culture of the central Balkans, named from the tell at Vinča-Belo Brdo on the Danube just east of today’s Belgrade. Its settlements, typified also at Pločnik and Divostin, left fine dark-burnished pottery, figurines, and one of Europe’s earliest copper-working traditions. The date range is archaeological, not a single people or state, and the culture’s finds spread into what is now Serbia, Bosnia, Romania, Bulgaria and North Macedonia. A set of incised signs on Vinča pottery has been read by some as a script; most specialists treat them as symbols, not writing. The culture is not drawn as a territorial outline on the globe.

items.name: Roman Singidunum and Sirmium
items.description: The future Serbian lands sat in Roman Moesia and Pannonia. Singidunum, a Scordisci foundation of the 3rd century BCE on the ridge where the Sava meets the Danube, became a legionary fortress and later a municipium; it is today’s Belgrade. Sirmium (Sremska Mitrovica) grew into one of the four capitals of the Tetrarchy (from 293) and a mint and imperial residence; several 4th-century emperors were proclaimed there, and Constantine was born at nearby Naissus (Niš). The Hun campaigns of the 440s wrecked the cities; Sirmium finally fell to the Avars in 582. Roman rule is already on the globe as the Roman Empire; this item is the local story, with pins at the cities, not a second outline.

items.name: Slavic settlement
items.description: South Slavic groups moved into the central Balkans in the 6th and 7th centuries, during and after the Avar khaganate, settling the river valleys and the ruins of Roman towns. Byzantine sources (Procopius, the Miracles of Saint Demetrius, later De Administrando Imperio) describe raids and then settlement; archaeology shows new cemeteries and pottery rather than a single invasion year. By the 7th century Slavic speech was established in the interior that later became Serbia. The Avar khaganate is already on the globe; this item is not drawn as a tribal outline, because the settlement was a process, not a bordered state.

items.name: The first Serbian principality
items.description: The first named Serbian princes appear in Constantine VII’s De Administrando Imperio: Višeslav, Radoslav, Prosigoj, and Vlastimir (mid-9th century), who fought off a Bulgarian attack and gave the Vlastimirović line its name. Under Mutimir the court accepted baptism from Byzantium (c. 870). Časlav (c. 927–960) briefly restored a larger principality after a period of Bulgarian rule, then the state broke up and Byzantium annexed the region around 969. The centre is usually placed in Raška, but the borders are too poorly mapped to draw; this item is timeline and pins only.

periods.name: Vlastimir and the baptism of the court

items.name: Raška
items.description: In the late 11th century a Serbian polity re-formed in the Raška region around Stari Ras (near today’s Novi Pazar), under Vukan (from c. 1091), who fought and treated with Alexios I Komnenos. His successors, including Uroš I and Uroš II, were usually Byzantine vassals and sometimes Hungarian allies, in a landscape still contested with Dioclea (Zeta). The grand župan Tihomir held Raška when his younger brother Nemanja, already given Toplica, Ibar and Rasina, rose against him. The globe’s medieval Serbia shape starts with Nemanja in 1166; this earlier Raška is too thinly mapped to draw on its own.

sources.title: Wikipedia — Vukan, Grand Prince of Serbia

items.name: Stefan Nemanja and the Grand Principality
items.description: Stefan Nemanja took power in Raška in 1166/68, survived a Byzantine counter-stroke, and after Manuel I’s death in 1180 expanded into Zeta, Kosovo and, for a time, Niš — where he met Frederick Barbarossa in 1189. He abdicated in 1196, took monastic vows as Simeon, and died at Hilandar on Athos in 1199; he was later canonised. His son Stefan (the First-Crowned) held the grand princely title until a papal crown arrived in 1217. Nemanja’s other son Rastko, as Sava, organised the church in the next period. This is the first Serbian state drawn on the globe, from the Raška core, then with Zeta and Kosovo.

items.name: The Nemanjić kingdom
items.description: In 1217 Stefan, Nemanja’s son, was crowned king; in 1219 his brother Sava obtained autocephaly for the Serbian Church from the Patriarchate of Nicaea, with its first seat at Žiča and later at Peć. The kingdom’s heart remained Raška, Kosovo and Zeta. Under Stefan Uroš II Milutin (1282–1321) Serbia took Skopje and much of northern Macedonia from Byzantium (1282) and became a regional power, building the monasteries at Gračanica and Hilandar’s later katholikon. Stefan Dečanski (Visoki Dečani) defeated Bulgaria at Velbazhd in 1330. His son Dušan deposed him in 1331 and ruled as king until the imperial coronation of 1346.

items.name: Dušan’s empire
items.description: On 16 April 1346 Stefan Dušan was crowned “emperor of the Serbs and Greeks” at Skopje, which he made his capital, and raised the Serbian Church to a patriarchate. By 1348 his armies held Macedonia, much of Albania, Epirus and Thessaly; Thessaloniki itself was never taken. His law code (Dušanov zakonik) was issued in 1349 and enlarged in 1354. He died on 20 December 1355. His son Stefan Uroš V could not hold the nobles; after the Ottoman victory at Maritsa (26 September 1371) and Uroš’s death the same year, the empire broke into regional lordships. The globe shows the 1348 peak and then shrinks to Lazar’s Moravian Serbia, not every successor.

items.name: Moravian Serbia and Kosovo
items.description: After 1371 Prince Lazar Hrebeljanović built a principality in the Morava valley, with its seat at Kruševac and a church centre at Ravanica. Vuk Branković held Kosovo, the Balšići Zeta; Lazar did not reunite the old empire. On 15 June 1389 (28 June in the modern civil calendar) Lazar’s army met the Ottomans under Murad I on Kosovo Field. Both Lazar and Murad were killed; the political result was Serbian vassalage under Lazar’s son Stefan Lazarević. The battle became the central story of later Serbian memory. In 1402, after Timur defeated the Ottomans at Ankara, Stefan turned toward Byzantium and Hungary and took the title of despot.

items.name: The Serbian Despotate
items.description: Stefan Lazarević, already a prince, received the Byzantine title of despot in 1402 and, from King Sigismund of Hungary in 1403, Belgrade, which he made his capital. His Law Code and the Resava (Manasija) monastery belong to this revival. On his death in 1427 Belgrade went back to Hungary; his successor Đurađ Branković, who also held the Kosovo lands, built a new fortress-capital at Smederevo (completed 1430). After a long Ottoman pressure — including the fall of Constantinople in 1453 — Smederevo surrendered on 20 June 1459. Medieval Serbia on the globe ends that year.

items.name: Ottoman Serbia
items.description: After 1459 the former despotate was organised as Ottoman sanjaks, above all the Sanjak of Smederevo (the Belgrade Pashalik). Some of the population converted to Islam; others lived as Christian rayah under the millet system, and boys were taken in the devşirme. Belgrade became a major fortress on the empire’s Hungarian frontier, falling to Süleyman in 1521. In 1690, after a Habsburg occupation collapsed, Patriarch Arsenije III led a large Serbian migration into Habsburg land (the first “Great Migration”). Janissary dahis in the Belgrade Pashalik, and their massacre of local knezes in January 1804, set off the First Serbian Uprising. On the globe the Ottoman Balkans ring covers this period at its height; it is not redrawn as a local eyalet.

sources.title: Wikipedia — Great Migrations of the Serbs

items.name: Habsburg interludes
items.description: Habsburg armies took Belgrade in 1688, during the Great Turkish War, then lost it in 1690, after which Patriarch Arsenije III led a large part of the Serbian population north into the empire (the Great Migration). The Treaty of Passarowitz (21 July 1718) created a Habsburg Kingdom of Serbia from the former Sanjak of Smederevo, ruled from Belgrade as a crown land, separate from the Banat and Syrmia. The Treaty of Belgrade (18 September 1739) gave it back to the Ottomans. A third occupation, Koča’s frontier, ran through the Austro-Turkish War of 1788–1791. Only the 1718–1739 kingdom is drawn on the globe; the earlier and later occupations are pins.

periods.name: Great Turkish War and the 1690 migration

items.name: The First Serbian Uprising
items.description: On 14 February 1804 village leaders at Orašac, in Šumadija, chose Karađorđe Petrović to lead a revolt against the janissary dahis who had murdered the district knezes. The rising became a war with the Ottoman Empire. The insurgents took Belgrade in 1806 and held most of the Belgrade Pashalik, creating a rough revolutionary state with an assembly and a governing council. A march on Niš failed at Čegar in 1809 (Stevan Sinđelić). In 1813, after Russia made peace with the Ottomans, an Ottoman army reconquered the pashalik and Karađorđe fled. This is the last Serbian polity drawn by the pack; it ends in 1813.

periods.name: Orašac to the taking of Belgrade

items.name: The Second Uprising and the autonomous principality
items.description: In April 1815 Miloš Obrenović raised a second revolt at Takovo. It was shorter and ended in a settlement: Miloš became the hereditary prince of an autonomous Principality of Serbia under Ottoman suzerainty, confirmed in 1830 and enlarged in 1833 (the six nahijas). The last Ottoman garrisons left in 1867. The 1815 settlement is the start of the principality the nations layer already draws from that year (as an Ottoman vassal until 1878), so the uprising is not given a second globe outline. Rivalry with the Karađorđević line, a first constitution (1835, quickly withdrawn) and the 1848 movements in the Habsburg south all belong to this principality.

items.name: Independence and the Kingdom of Serbia
items.description: The Congress of Berlin (1878) recognised Serbia as an independent state and awarded it Niš, Pirot and Vranje. Prince Milan declared a kingdom in 1882. A disputed succession ended in the May Coup of 1903, which brought Peter I Karađorđević to the throne and a more parliamentary regime. In the Balkan Wars (1912–13) Serbia took Kosovo, Vardar Macedonia and part of the Sandžak. In the First World War it was overrun in 1915 after a famous 1914 defence, the army retreated through Albania, and it returned in 1918. On 1 December 1918 Prince Regent Alexander proclaimed the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes. From 1815 these years are on the nations layer, not this pack’s outlines.

periods.name: Balkan Wars and the First World War

items.name: Yugoslavia
items.description: The Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes (renamed Yugoslavia in 1929) united the pre-war Serbian kingdom with the south Slav lands of the former Austria-Hungary, with its capital at Belgrade. A royal dictatorship (1929), the assassination of King Alexander in 1934, and the 1941 Axis invasion followed. Occupied Serbia and a wider civil war ended with Josip Broz Tito’s Partisans in power; the court never returned. The Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia (from 1945, formally 1963) was a six-republic federation with Serbia one of them, and two autonomous provinces (Vojvodina and Kosovo) inside it. After Tito’s death in 1980 the federation strained; in 1991 Slovenia and Croatia declared independence and the state began to break up.

sources.title: Wikipedia — Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia

items.name: The 1990s wars and Kosovo
items.description: As Yugoslavia broke up, Serbia under Slobodan Milošević was the core of the rump Federal Republic of Yugoslavia (1992) and was involved in the wars in Croatia and Bosnia (1991–95). In Kosovo, an Albanian majority insurgency (the KLA) and a Serbian counter-insurgency led to NATO’s bombing campaign against the FR Yugoslavia (24 March–10 June 1999) and to UN administration of Kosovo (UNMIK) under Resolution 1244. Milošević fell in October 2000. Montenegro left the state union in 2006; on 17 February 2008 Kosovo’s assembly declared independence, which Serbia does not recognise and which a part of the UN membership has recognised. The wars and the status of Kosovo remain the most contested part of the recent record; the item follows standard published chronology.

items.name: The Republic of Serbia
items.description: When Montenegro voted for independence in May 2006, the state union ended and the Republic of Serbia became a separate state, the formal successor of the union, with Belgrade as its capital. It is a parliamentary republic, a candidate for European Union membership (negotiations opened in 2014), and a UN member. Kosovo’s 2008 declaration, which Serbia rejects, and the Brussels dialogue with Priština have been the central foreign-policy dispute. The country covers the territory of the former Socialist Republic of Serbia, including Vojvodina; Kosovo is administered separately. The nations layer already shows these borders from 2006 (and without Kosovo from 2008, following the layer’s usual practice of drawing declared independent states).
